Key Takeaways

Cathie Wood's ARK Invest bought 549,659 shares of CoreWeave on Friday in two of its ETFs, ARKK and ARKW. That's about $22 million at Friday's close.

CoreWeave trades at 0.9x forward sales, its lowest point in the past year and far below its 3.4x average, while analysts expect its revenue to reach $27.1 billion in 2027.

Oracle, another AI cloud, faces the same test: whether demand for AI computing pays back the cost of building it.

On price, the numbers back the buy, and the yield on CoreWeave's next contract-backed loan is the figure to watch.

Cathie Wood just added to one of AI's most beaten-up stocks. ARK Invest's daily trade email shows it bought 549,659 shares of CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ) on Friday, when the stock was 71% below its 52-week high.

CoreWeave isn't the only AI cloud investors are doubting. One of its rivals faces the same question about who will fill its new capacity. Oracle (ORCL:NYSE), which rose with CoreWeave's last jump, is building its own AI cloud around contracts with OpenAI.

A small add in two funds

ARK split the buy between two ETFs: 432,596 shares went into the ARK Innovation ETF (ARKK) and 117,063 into the ARK Next Generation Internet ETF (ARKW). The new shares are 0.12% of ARKK and 0.13% of ARKW. At Friday's $39.51 close, the 549,659 shares come to about $22 million. That's the share count times the close, since the email doesn't say what ARK paid.

CoreWeave was already a meaningful holding. ARK's 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 13, showed 4.21 million shares worth $367 million. That was 2.1% of its 13F stocks and its 15th-largest position. It was also 58% more shares than ARK held three months earlier. The filing doesn't show what ARK did between Sept. 30 and Friday, and CoreWeave's share price fell 55% from its quarter-end level to Friday's close.

Musk Warns AI's "Cash Shortage Is Also Going to Be Nuts Next Year." Credit Markets Put SpaceX Beside Oracle ©NASA/Aubrey Gemignani and Nikada from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

Elon Musk warned on X that AI's compute delays will take "hundreds of billions of incremental dollars just for working capital" next year.

SpaceX relies more on outside credit than its CFO's self-funding message suggests.

J.P. Morgan's credit default swap data puts SpaceX beside Oracle at about 275 basis points, against about 80 for Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon.

Analysts expect SpaceX's free cash flow to be negative $146 billion in 2027.

SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) CEO Elon Musk has a warning for everyone building AI data centers. It may apply to his own company most of all.

He posted on X:

"The cash shortage is also going to be nuts next year. Even cumulative industry delays of a few months between paying for compute and getting it reliable enough to generate revenue will mean hundreds of billions of incremental dollars just for working capital. Where will that come from?"

For SpaceX, credit markets have a pretty good guess: lenders.

SpaceX lands in the "credit-dependent" tier

One investor laid out J.P. Morgan's credit default swap data on X. Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ), Alphabet (GOOG) and Amazon trade at about 80 basis points, "with enough cash flow to fund most of their CapEx." SpaceX and Oracle (ORCL:NYSE) sit at about 275 basis points, "with buildouts increasingly reliant on outside funding."

That means insuring SpaceX's debt costs about 3.4x as much as insuring Microsoft's.

This week's bond sale backs that up. SpaceX sold $32 billion of debt backed by Nvidia chips, and people familiar with the sale say the biggest piece, about $25.2 billion, priced at 8.259%. The average US high-grade bond yielded 5.95% that day, according to Bloomberg's index data.

TIKR tracks 40 analysts on SpaceX. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on SpaceX, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See SpaceX's Analyst Ratings

Analysts don't see the cash flow yet

CFO Bret Johnsen said this week that much of the 10 gigawatts SpaceX plans to build next year will be funded from internal cash flows, as another investor relayed it on X. Analysts' estimates show far more cash going out than coming in:

SpaceX (SPCX): free cash flow, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2026-2028 (TIKR)

That adds up to nearly $270 billion of negative free cash flow from 2026 through 2028, with $146 billion of it in 2027, the year of the 10-gigawatt build. SpaceX held $89.9 billion of cash and marketable securities at Sept. 30, and it has guided to $35 billion to $40 billion of capex in the fourth quarter alone.

title: Intuit vs. Oracle: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
detail:
Intuit vs. Oracle: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?
Sara Appino, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 21, 2026 at 5:00 PM MST 6 min read
INTU
ORCL
AAPL
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Investors often find themselves choosing between specialized software leaders and broad infrastructure giants. Deciding whether to buy Intuit (NASDAQ:INTU) or Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) depends on your preference for consumer stability versus enterprise growth.

Intuit serves as the backbone for personal and small business finances, while Oracle provides the essential databases and cloud infrastructure that large organizations require. Both companies are currently integrating artificial intelligence to enhance their platforms. This comparison examines their growth rates, balance sheets, and relative valuations to determine which stock fits best in a 2027 outlook.

The case for Intuit

Intuit provides essential financial technology solutions for millions of global consumers and small businesses through its core brands like TurboTax, QuickBooks, and Credit Karma. The company currently serves approximately 93 million users and relies on major distribution platforms like the Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) App Store and Google Play Store. To support its vast software ecosystem, it maintains strategic partnerships with major cloud infrastructure providers including Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) and Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG).

In the 12 months ended Oct. 31, 2026, revenue reached nearly $21.9 billion, representing growth of close to 12.8% compared to the prior twelve-month period. Net income for this time frame was approximately $4.8 billion, reflecting the company's ability to maintain high net margins while expanding its user base. This steady financial expansion is largely driven by consistent, recurring demand for its digital accounting and tax preparation platforms among mid-market businesses.

As of its July 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is nearly 0.4x, a metric that compares total debt against the value of shareholder equity to assess financial leverage. The current ratio is approximately 1.5x, reflecting a healthy ability to pay short-term obligations using its most liquid assets. In the fiscal year ended July 31, 2026, free cash flow reached nearly $8.7 billion, though note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 23.3% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for Oracle

Oracle offers enterprise software, cloud applications, and infrastructure services through a global delivery model that serves corporations, government agencies, and educational institutions. The company distributes its complex database systems and cloud applications in more than 145 countries and operates through a network of resellers and system integrators. It recently focused on expanding its presence in tech stocks by building out massive data center capacity specifically designed for high-performance artificial intelligence workloads.

Steven Porrello, The Motley Fool

Trading disclosure

Earlier this year, things seemed to be going exactly right for fuel-cell manufacturer Bloom Energy (NYSE:BE).

It's not hard to see why. The race to build AI data centers had stimulated such an enormous appetite for electricity that developers, facing grid bottlenecks and tight construction timelines, simply couldn't afford to wait years for traditional power grid connections.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

In that context, new orders for Bloom's fuel-cell systems were coming in hot: First Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) contracted for 1.2 gigawatts (GW) of capacity, then Brookfield Asset Management (NYSE:BAM) expanded its financing framework with Bloom for AI projects from $5 billion to a whopping $25 billion.

Both were significant developments for Bloom's business, and Wall Street absolutely agreed: The stock soared to an all-time high of roughly $350, more than quadrupling in value from where it started the year.

If you take a look at Bloom's stock chart today, however, you'll see a different picture: It has fallen from its high to roughly $168 per share.

That raises the obvious question: What the heck is happening? And, more importantly, should you take this as an occasion to buy Bloom stock?

Is Bloom Energy still worth buying?

For starters, Bloom is a fuel cell manufacturer. In simple terms, it makes equipment that let data centers and other customers generate electricity on-site rather than waiting years to connect to the grid. These fuel cells are also a source of (relatively) clean power: Instead of burning fuel, they use an electrochemical reaction to convert fuel (such as natural gas) into electricity. It's a pretty neat concept, and it is especially useful for those who need round-the-clock power.

As mentioned, Bloom stock soared earlier this year as sales of Bloom boxes went through the roof. This hasn't changed. Indeed, third-quarter sales surged 138% year over year to $1.24 billion, prompting management (yet again!) to raise full-year revenue guidance to between $4.4 billion and $4.6 billion. For perspective, its full-year 2025 revenue was about $2 billion.

What has changed, however, is the environment, or more specifically: Wall Street's willingness to pay sky-high valuations for companies associated with the AI boom. Investors have become increasingly concerned about the billions being poured into AI infrastructure, and Bloom, whose future growth is tied to AI spending, has found itself caught in this broader wave of bearish sentiment.

Nvidia (NASDAQ: $NVDA) plunged 14% on Friday and the Nasdaq Composite lost 5.3%, capping the index's worst week since 2020 as investors questioned whether the trillions of dollars being poured into artificial intelligence will pay off. The rout dragged Bitcoin (CRYPTO: $BTC) to its lowest levels since the summer.

The selloff marks the biggest test yet for the AI boom that has driven markets for three years. Analysts are now divided over whether it is a healthy correction or the start of a dot-com-style bust.

The Nasdaq closed at 22,617.73, about 18% below its Oct. 6 record and down 10% for the week, erasing its gains for 2026. The S&P 500 slipped into correction territory.

Nvidia closed at $125.53, down 47.5% from its October record of $239.24, after losing nearly 23% over the week. The chipmaker beat earnings estimates and raised its outlook on Tuesday, but those results have done little to slow the slide following Jensen Huang's departure as CEO.

The losses extended across AI suppliers and infrastructure firms. CoreWeave (NASDAQ: $CRWV) closed at $39.51, nearly 80% below its 2025 peak, while Oracle (NYSE: $ORCL) is down about 70% from its highs. AMD (NASDAQ: $AMD) fell 20.5% for the week, and the iShares Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ: $SOXX) dropped 17.4%.

Newly listed Anthropic (NASDAQ: $ANT), which raised $81 billion in the largest IPO on record, closed its first day 17% above its $83 offering price before falling about 9% on Friday.

Crypto has been pulled down with tech. Bitcoin ended the week near $58,895, down 9.8% for the week and more than 50% below its 2025 peak, while the total crypto market value fell to about $2.01 trillion, half its peak. The Crypto Fear and Greed Index dropped to 9, signaling extreme fear. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs saw $582.2 million in net outflows on Thursday.

Some prominent voices see a bubble. Owen Lamont, a portfolio manager at Acadian Asset Management, told Fortune he now sees a 70% chance the U.S. stock market is in one, after arguing in January that it was not. Bank of America's November fund manager survey showed investors cutting tech exposure by the most since 2006.

Others see a reset rather than a collapse. Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners, called it an "AI repricing" tied to slowing data center construction and tighter funding, Reuters reported. Lawrence Gillum, chief fixed income strategist at LPL Financial, said the decline was "not a bubble bursting."

Today's big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks?

Dell reports its quarterly results on Tuesday, Nov 24, after the market closes. Last quarter it booked $60.9 billion of AI server orders. It ended the quarter with a $95 billion backlog, meaning orders booked but not yet delivered. In May 2024, the backlog was $3.8 billion.

Can those orders still make money? Dell buys memory chips for these servers, and memory has become dearer. Shares of the memory maker Micron are up 206% in a year.

Dell's stock has fallen 9.3% this week, to $312.54 at Thursday's close. Other AI hardware stocks fell with it. HPE fell 5.8% and Micron 11.3%. Dell is now about 47% below its high.

Report days move Dell's stock a lot. Over its last 12 reports, the median next-day move was 10.6%, up or down. The median is the middle result. Six of those moves were up and six were down. The worst was a 17.9% fall.

Dell sits about 47% below its high, and one report day can move it 10% or more. If you are waiting for a better price to buy, your cash does not have to sit idle. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays.

Is Dell Keeping Less Of Each Sales Dollar?

Dell's sales have grown fast, but its gross margin has slipped. Gross margin is the share of sales left after the direct cost of making the products. Sales grew 93% from the quarter to Nov 2024 to the quarter to Jul 2026. Gross profit grew 85%.

Why does the margin slip? An AI server is mostly parts made by other companies. These are Nvidia's chips and the memory that sits beside them. So Dell keeps fewer cents per dollar on AI servers than on the rest of its business.

AI servers are also a growing share of Dell's sales. Dell expects $74.0 billion of AI server sales in fiscal 2027, the year to January 2027. It sold $32.5 billion in the first half. That leaves about $20.7 billion a quarter for the second half. Last quarter it sold $16.4 billion. More AI servers and dearer memory both push the margin down.

So far the market has not minded. Dell's two best report days this year came after quarters in which its gross margin fell. The stock rose 21.9% in February and 32.8% in May.
